why_how.text: Passing follows a set order: look ahead and behind, signal, then sound the horn, and the horn puts the driver ahead under a duty to help.
The law fixes the clearance at two feet, and the handbook sets five hundred feet of sight on curves and hills.

scenario.text: Dana wants to pass a slow car on a hill and can see only about three hundred feet ahead.

reasoning.text: The handbook says not to pass on a curve or hill where you cannot see at least five hundred feet ahead.

result.text: Dana stays behind until the road ahead is visible for at least five hundred feet and no solid yellow line is in Dana's lane.

claim.text: Common mistake: mixing up the two-foot passing clearance with the five-hundred-foot sight distance.

correction.text: Passing clearance is at least two feet to the left of the passed vehicle, while the sight distance on a curve or hill is at least five hundred feet.

prompt.text: Dana is on a hill with about three hundred feet of view ahead and a slow car in front. May Dana pass?

answer.text: No. Passing on a curve or hill needs at least five hundred feet of sight.

rationale.text: The handbook sets five hundred feet of sight on curves and hills, and three hundred feet falls short.

narration.text: This chapter covers passing, parking, backing, intersections and roundabouts. It opens with passing, which the handbook breaks into clear steps and clear limits. In this lesson you will review the order of steps before a pass, the legal duty that a horn signal creates, the room and sight distance a pass requires, the two-foot clearance the law sets, the places where passing is never safe, the yellow line markings that forbid it, and the duties of the driver who is being passed. Each rule comes straight from the handbook, so read the exact wording closely.

lines.text: The horn creates a duty to help.

narration.text: To pass, the handbook sets an order. First, look ahead and behind to judge whether it is safe. Then signal to the drivers around you. Then sound the horn to alert the driver ahead. That horn signal matters legally. Your horn signal puts the driver you are passing under a legal duty to help you get by. So the three steps run look, signal, horn, and the horn turns the other driver from a bystander into someone with a duty to help the pass succeed. Keep the order straight, because questions may scramble it and ask which step comes first.

lines.text: Plenty of room and a steady speed.
See far enough to get back in.
At least two feet to the left.

narration.text: The handbook says to pass only with plenty of room and a steady speed, and only if you can see far enough to get back into your lane before meeting oncoming traffic. While passing, the law requires the passing driver to stay at least two feet to the left of the vehicle being passed. So two separate conditions apply at once. Ahead of you, there must be enough room and enough view to finish the pass. Beside you, there must be at least two feet between your car and the car you are passing for the whole time you are alongside it.

lines.text: Curves or hills under five hundred feet.
Solid yellow line in your lane.

narration.text: Some places rule passing out. Railroad crossings, town and city intersections, and marked intersections in the countryside are places where passing is never safe and is usually against the law. Do not pass on a curve or hill where you cannot see at least five hundred feet ahead. And do not pass where a solid yellow line is in your lane or where there is a double solid yellow line. So before any pass, run three checks: am I near a crossing or intersection, can I see five hundred feet on this curve or hill, and is there a solid yellow line on my side?

lines.text: Clearance beside: at least two feet.
Sight ahead on curves or hills: five hundred.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two passing distances appear in the handbook, and they measure different things. Passing clearance is at least two feet to the left of the passed vehicle, while the sight distance needed to pass on a curve or hill is at least five hundred feet. Practice questions may swap them, offering five hundred feet as the clearance or two feet as the sight distance. Ask what the question measures. Space beside the car you pass means two feet. How far you must see ahead on a curve or hill means five hundred feet. Keep each number tied to its measurement.

lines.text: Speeding up into a crash is a misdemeanor.

narration.text: The other half of passing belongs to the driver being passed. When someone is passing you, you must help: move toward the right edge if they sound the horn, and never speed up. Speeding up and failing to give way to a passing vehicle is a misdemeanor if it leads to a crash with injury or property damage. So the duties split cleanly. When passing, you signal your intention and blow the horn to alert the driver ahead; when being passed, you must help by moving to the right edge of the road if the passing driver blows the horn, and you must never increase your speed. Questions often describe the driver being passed and ask what that driver must do.

lines.text: A slow car ahead on a hill.
About three hundred feet of view.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Dana is driving up a hill behind a slow car and can see only about three hundred feet ahead. The center line is broken on Dana's side. May Dana pass? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. The handbook says not to pass on a curve or hill where you cannot see at least five hundred feet ahead, and three hundred feet falls short of that. Dana stays behind until the view ahead reaches at least five hundred feet, then looks, signals and sounds the horn before passing, keeping at least two feet of clearance.

lines.text: Two feet beside; five hundred ahead on hills.

narration.text: Let us recap. Before passing, look ahead and behind, signal, then sound the horn, and that horn signal puts the driver ahead under a legal duty to help. Pass only with plenty of room, a steady speed, and enough view to get back before oncoming traffic, keeping at least two feet to the left of the passed vehicle. Never pass at railroad crossings or intersections, on curves or hills without five hundred feet of sight, or where a solid yellow line is in your lane. When you are passed, move right and never speed up; speeding up into a crash is a misdemeanor.

why_how.text: The handbook bans passing on the right except where allowed, because it puts you on the other driver's blind side.
The allowed cases are listed: multi-lane highways, one-way streets, beside a left-turning car, and from a right-turn lane.

scenario.text: Lee is on a two-lane road behind a car that has stopped in a left-turn lane to wait for a gap.

reasoning.text: Passing on the right is allowed around a car in a left-turn lane.

result.text: Lee may pass the waiting car on the right in this case.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking passing on the right is never allowed.

correction.text: Passing on the right is generally illegal, but it is allowed on roads with two or more lanes each way, on one-way streets, beside a left-turning car, and from a right-turn lane.

prompt.text: Lee is behind a car waiting in a left-turn lane. May Lee pass it on the right?

answer.text: Yes. Passing on the right is allowed around a car in a left-turn lane.

rationale.text: Passing on the right is generally banned, but a car in a left-turn lane is one of the listed exceptions.

narration.text: This short lesson focuses on one question: when may you pass on the right? The handbook's answer has two parts. First, a general rule that passing on the right is illegal except where specifically allowed, along with the handbook's reason for that rule. Second, a list of specific situations where passing on the right is allowed. You will also review the special rule for three-lane highways, where the center lane may be used for passing only under certain markings. Learn the exceptions as a list, because practice questions often present one of them and ask whether the pass is legal.

lines.text: You end up on the driver's blind side.
That car may turn right or pull over.

narration.text: Passing on the right is illegal except where specifically allowed. The handbook gives the reason: it puts you on the other driver's blind side, where that car might turn right or pull over. So the default answer to whether you may pass on the right is no. Only when a situation matches one of the listed exceptions does that answer change. When you are studying this rule, keep both halves together: the ban itself, and the blind-side reason the handbook attaches to it. Questions sometimes ask why passing on the right is restricted, and the blind side is the answer the handbook gives.

lines.text: Two or more lanes each way.
Beside a left turner, or from a right-turn lane.

narration.text: The handbook lists the cases where passing on the right is allowed. It is allowed on highways with two or more lanes each way, on one-way streets, around a car in a left-turn lane, and when you are in a lane reserved for right turns. So a driver on a four-lane highway may pass on the right, a driver on a one-way street may pass on the right, a driver behind a car waiting to turn left may go around it on the right, and a driver in a right-turn lane may move past cars in the lane beside it. Outside those cases, the general ban applies.

Here is the trap. Practice questions push learners toward one of two extremes: that passing on the right is always fine when traffic is slow, or that it is never allowed. Neither matches the handbook. Passing on the right is generally illegal, but it is allowed on roads with two or more lanes each way, on one-way streets, beside a left-turning car, and from a right-turn lane. So when a question describes a pass on the right, check it against the list. If the situation is on the list, the pass is allowed. If it is not, the general ban applies.

lines.text: A car waits in a left-turn lane.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Lee is driving on a two-lane road when the car ahead stops in a left-turn lane to wait for a gap in oncoming traffic. May Lee pass the waiting car on the right? Work it out before reading on. The answer is yes. Passing on the right is generally illegal, but the handbook lists passing around a car in a left-turn lane as one of the allowed cases. Lee may pass it on the right. If the car ahead were simply driving slowly on that two-lane road, the general ban would apply instead. The left-turn lane case is on the list.

lines.text: Multi-lane, one-way, left turner, right-turn lane.
Three lanes: marked center lane only.

narration.text: To wrap up, passing on the right is illegal except where specifically allowed, because it puts you on the other driver's blind side, where that car might turn right or pull over. It is allowed on highways with two or more lanes each way, on one-way streets, around a car in a left-turn lane, and from a lane reserved for right turns. On a three-lane highway, you may pass only in the center lane where it is marked for passing your way, unless the car in the center lane is turning left. Next, the rules for parking. Outside the list, do not pass on the right.

why_how.text: The handbook sets where to park, how to pull out, and a list of places and distances where parking is barred.
Several parking distances are fixed in feet or blocks, and they differ by what you are near.

scenario.text: Kai wants to park on a city street about ten feet from a fire hydrant.

reasoning.text: The handbook says not to park within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant or of a fire station entrance.

result.text: Kai moves the car so it sits at least fifteen feet from the hydrant.

claim.text: Common mistake: using the twenty-five foot cross-street distance for fire hydrants too.

correction.text: The no-parking distance is fifteen feet from a fire hydrant but twenty-five feet from the curb line of a cross street.

prompt.text: Kai parks ten feet from a fire hydrant on a city street. Is that allowed?

answer.text: No. Parking within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant is not allowed.

rationale.text: The hydrant distance is fifteen feet, separate from the twenty-five foot cross-street distance.

lines.text: Which side and how to pull out.

narration.text: This lesson collects the handbook's parking rules. You will review which side of the street to park on, how to pull out of a parallel space, the places where parking is never allowed, the set distances from cross streets and fire hydrants, the rules for highway shoulders, how far to stay from a fire or fire truck, the ban on parking in an interstate right of way, and who may use disabled parking spaces. Several of these rules carry numbers in feet or blocks. Practice questions often swap those numbers, so pay attention to which distance belongs to which place.

lines.text: Park on the right unless one-way.
Look, then signal left to pull out.
No signal needed on the left of a one-way.

narration.text: Park on the right-hand side of the street at all times, unless it is a one-way street. When pulling out of a parallel space, look for approaching traffic and signal a left turn first. The signal is not needed when you are parked on the left of a one-way street. So on an ordinary two-way street, you park on the right and signal left as you pull out into traffic. On a one-way street, parking on the left can be allowed, and pulling out from that left side does not call for the left signal. Questions may describe either situation and ask what to do.

lines.text: At an intersection or in front of a driveway.
On a crosswalk, sidewalk or bridge.
Never on the paved travel lanes.

narration.text: Some places are always off limits. Do not park at an intersection, in front of a driveway, or on a crosswalk, sidewalk or bridge. Never park on the paved travel part of a highway, and parking on the shoulder is illegal unless drivers from both directions can see your vehicle for at least two hundred feet. Parking is not allowed anywhere in an interstate right of way, except in designated areas or in an emergency. And disabled parking spaces may be used only by a vehicle showing a disability license plate or placard. Each of these is a firm rule rather than a suggestion.

lines.text: Cross street curb line: twenty-five feet.
No curb: fifteen feet from right of way lines.
Hydrant or fire station: fifteen feet.

narration.text: Two distances deal with corners and fire equipment. Do not park within twenty-five feet of the curb line of a cross street, or within fifteen feet of the intersecting right of way lines where there is no curb. Do not park within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant or of a fire station entrance. So near a corner with a curb, stay twenty-five feet back from the cross street curb line. Near a corner with no curb, the distance from the right of way lines is fifteen feet. And near a hydrant or a fire station entrance, the distance is fifteen feet as well.

lines.text: Cross street curb line: twenty-five feet.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The no-parking distance is fifteen feet from a fire hydrant but twenty-five feet from the curb line of a cross street, and fifteen feet from the right of way lines where there is no curb. Practice questions may offer twenty-five feet for a hydrant or fifteen feet for a curbed corner. Tie each number to its place. If the question mentions a hydrant or a fire station entrance, the answer is fifteen feet. If it mentions the curb line of a cross street, the answer is twenty-five feet. Only a corner without a curb uses fifteen feet for the cross street.

lines.text: Fire in a city: one block.
Fire outside a city: four hundred feet.
Shoulder: seen two hundred feet both ways.

narration.text: When parking, keep at least one block away from a fire or fire truck inside city limits, and at least four hundred feet away outside a city. That is a different rule from the shoulder rule. Parking on a highway shoulder is illegal unless drivers from both directions can see your vehicle for at least two hundred feet. So three figures sit close together in this part of the handbook. Near a fire in a city, think one block. Near a fire outside a city, think four hundred feet. On a shoulder, think of being visible for two hundred feet in both directions.

Here is a quick check: Kai finds an open spot on a city street, but the car would sit about ten feet from a fire hydrant. The spot is not near a corner. Is parking there allowed? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. The handbook says not to park within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant or of a fire station entrance, and ten feet falls inside that distance. Kai needs a spot at least fifteen feet from the hydrant. The twenty-five foot distance would apply only to the curb line of a cross street, which is a separate rule.

lines.text: Park right; signal left to pull out.
Fire: a block in town, four hundred feet outside.

narration.text: Let us recap. Park on the right unless the street is one-way, and look and signal left when pulling out of a parallel space. Never park at an intersection, in front of a driveway, or on a crosswalk, sidewalk or bridge. Stay twenty-five feet from a cross street curb line, fifteen feet from right of way lines with no curb, and fifteen feet from a hydrant or fire station entrance. Never park on the paved travel lanes, and on a shoulder only if visible for two hundred feet both ways. Near a fire, keep a block away in town and four hundred feet outside.

why_how.text: The handbook says children and small objects behind a vehicle are hard to see from the driver's seat, so you check before getting in.
A vehicle is harder to control and stop in reverse, so the handbook sets a slow backing speed.

scenario.text: Jamie needs to back out of a driveway where neighborhood children often play.

reasoning.text: Before getting in, check behind the vehicle for children or small objects; then steer with the left hand and look over the right shoulder through the rear window.

result.text: Jamie walks behind the car first, then backs out at no more than ten miles per hour while looking through the rear window.

claim.text: Common mistake: backing up using only the mirrors.

correction.text: The backing speed of no more than ten miles per hour pairs with looking over the right shoulder through the rear window, not just in the mirrors.

prompt.text: Jamie is about to back out of a driveway. How fast may Jamie back, and where should Jamie look?

answer.text: No more than ten miles per hour, looking over the right shoulder through the rear window.

rationale.text: The handbook pairs the slow backing speed with looking back through the rear window rather than relying only on mirrors.

narration.text: This short lesson covers backing. The handbook gives three steps that work together. Before you even get into the vehicle, you check behind it. Once you are backing, you steer and look in a particular way. And throughout, you keep your speed very low. The handbook gives a reason for the first step, that children and small objects are hard to see from the driver's seat, and a reason for the last, that a vehicle is harder to control and stop in reverse. Keep each step and its reason together as you study, because questions may ask about either one.

lines.text: Look for children and small objects.
They are hard to see from the seat.

narration.text: Before getting in to back up, check behind the vehicle for children or small objects, which are hard to see from the driver's seat. This check happens outside the car, before you sit down. Once you are in the driver's seat, the area just behind the vehicle is difficult to see, according to the handbook. So the walk around the back is the first step of every backing move. Questions about backing often start with this step, asking what you should do first. The handbook's answer is to check behind the vehicle before getting in.

lines.text: No more than ten miles per hour.

narration.text: When backing, steer with your left hand and look over your right shoulder through the rear window, instead of relying only on the mirrors or the side window. Back up very slowly, at no more than ten miles per hour, because a vehicle is harder to control and stop in reverse. So the technique has three parts: left hand on the wheel, eyes over the right shoulder and out the rear window, and a speed of ten miles per hour or less. Mirrors and the side window are not enough on their own, according to the handbook. Use the rear window, not only mirrors.

lines.text: Keep it at ten or less.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers back up while watching only the mirrors. The handbook says to look over your right shoulder through the rear window instead of relying only on the mirrors or the side window. The backing speed of no more than ten miles per hour pairs with that rule. On practice questions, an option that backs up quickly, or that relies only on mirrors, does not match the handbook. The correct combination is a slow speed and a look back through the rear window. Memory line: slow, and look back. Ten miles per hour is the most.

Here is a quick check: Jamie is about to back out of a driveway where neighborhood children often play. Jamie has already walked behind the car and checked for children and small objects. How fast may Jamie back up, and where should Jamie look? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no more than ten miles per hour, steering with the left hand and looking over the right shoulder through the rear window. The handbook says not to rely only on the mirrors or the side window, and to back up very slowly because a vehicle is harder to control and stop in reverse.

lines.text: Left hand, right shoulder, rear window.
Ten miles per hour or less.

narration.text: To finish, before getting in to back up, check behind the vehicle for children or small objects, which are hard to see from the driver's seat. When backing, steer with your left hand and look over your right shoulder through the rear window, instead of relying only on the mirrors or the side window. Back up very slowly, at no more than ten miles per hour, because a vehicle is harder to control and stop in reverse. The slow speed and the look back through the rear window go together. Next, intersections and right of way.

why_how.text: The handbook says intersections are where crashes happen most often, with over one-third of fatal crashes occurring there.
The law requires slowing approaching an intersection even with the right of way, and sets an order at uncontrolled intersections.

scenario.text: At an intersection with no signs or signals, Riley and another driver arrive at the same moment, with the other car on Riley's right.

reasoning.text: When vehicles reach an uncontrolled intersection at the same moment, the vehicle on the right has the right of way.

result.text: Riley yields to the car on the right, then proceeds after slowing and checking the intersection.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking that having the right of way means you may go through an intersection without slowing.

correction.text: Having the right of way still requires you to slow down approaching the intersection and to avoid hitting anyone.

prompt.text: Riley and another car reach an uncontrolled intersection at the same moment, and the other car is on Riley's right. Who goes first?

rationale.text: When two vehicles arrive together at an uncontrolled intersection, the vehicle on the right has the right of way.

narration.text: The handbook calls intersections the place where crashes happen most often, and says over one-third of fatal motor vehicle crashes occur there. This lesson reviews the handbook's intersection rules. You will learn when a divided highway counts as two intersections, the duty to slow down even with the right of way, the order of right of way at intersections with no signs or signals, the rule against changing lanes inside an intersection, what to do at a stop sign and when leaving a driveway, and what a single-point interchange is. The right of way order is the most tested part.

lines.text: Slow down approaching, even with right of way.
Median wider than thirty feet: two intersections.

narration.text: The law requires you to slow down as you approach an intersection, even when you have the right of way. On a four-lane highway divided by a median wider than thirty feet, each crossing counts as a separate intersection, so you treat each half as its own intersection. And never change lanes while driving straight through an intersection. Those three rules apply wherever you meet cross traffic. Slowing is required, a wide median splits one crossing into two, and lane changes wait until you are past the intersection. Questions may test any of these as a single fact.

title.text: Right of way still means slowing

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers believe that having the right of way lets them roll through an intersection at full speed. The handbook says otherwise. Having the right of way still requires you to slow down approaching the intersection and to avoid hitting anyone. The law requires slowing as you approach an intersection even when you have the right of way. So on practice questions, an option that says a driver with the right of way may proceed without slowing is wrong. The right of way decides who should go first, but it never removes the duty to slow and to avoid a crash.

lines.text: Arriving together: vehicle on the right.
Facing cars: the left turner waits.

narration.text: At an intersection with no signs or signals, a vehicle already inside the intersection goes before one that has not entered. When vehicles reach an uncontrolled intersection at the same moment, the vehicle on the right has the right of way. And when two facing vehicles arrive together and one wants to turn left, the turning driver must signal and wait, so the driver going straight has the right of way. So the order runs: the car already inside first, then the car on the right when two arrive together, and when facing cars arrive together, straight traffic before the left turner.

lines.text: Right goes first when arriving together.
Left turner waits for straight traffic.

narration.text: Here is the second trap. The three uncontrolled-intersection rules are easy to blend. At an uncontrolled intersection the car already inside goes first, and when two arrive together the car on the right goes first; facing cars split straight-versus-left, with the left turner waiting. Practice questions may describe two cars arriving together and offer the car on the left, or describe a left turner and a straight driver and give the turn priority. Sort the situation first: is one car already inside, are the cars arriving from different directions, or are they facing each other? Then apply the matching rule.

lines.text: Stop completely, yield to through traffic.
Driveway: stop and yield to everyone.
Single-point interchange: one set of signals.

narration.text: At a stop sign you must stop completely and yield to traffic on the through street before moving on or turning. When coming out of a private driveway, stop and yield to every vehicle and pedestrian, and at a blind unmarked intersection stop and then creep forward carefully. The handbook also describes a single-point interchange, which merges two intersections into one above or below a free-flowing road, run by a single set of traffic signals. So stop signs and driveways both call for a full stop and yielding, and a single-point interchange is one signal-controlled intersection serving both directions.

Here is a quick check: Riley reaches an intersection with no signs or signals at the same moment as another car, which is approaching from Riley's right. Neither car has entered the intersection yet. Who goes first? Work it out before reading on. The answer is the car on Riley's right. When vehicles reach an uncontrolled intersection at the same moment, the vehicle on the right has the right of way. If the other car had already been inside the intersection, it would go first for that reason. Either way, Riley slows down approaching the intersection, as the law requires.

lines.text: Slow down, even with right of way.
Inside, then right, then straight over left.
Stop fully at signs and driveways.

narration.text: To wrap up, intersections are where crashes happen most often, with over one-third of fatal crashes occurring there. Slow down approaching any intersection, even with the right of way, and never change lanes inside one. A median wider than thirty feet makes two intersections. At uncontrolled intersections, the car already inside goes first, the car on the right goes first when two arrive together, and a left turner waits for straight traffic. Stop completely at stop signs and when leaving driveways, and a single-point interchange runs two intersections on one set of signals.

why_how.text: The handbook says a modern roundabout is smaller than a traffic circle and keeps speeds low, which makes it safer.
In both circles and roundabouts, traffic already circulating has the right of way over traffic entering.

scenario.text: Morgan approaches a single-lane roundabout and sees a bicyclist already circulating to the left.

reasoning.text: On entry you yield to any vehicles or bicyclists already circulating.

result.text: Morgan slows, yields to the bicyclist, then enters and later signals before exiting.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking circulating traffic in a roundabout must yield to cars waiting to enter.

correction.text: Entering traffic yields to vehicles and bicyclists already inside, while circulating traffic does not yield to approaching cars but does yield to pedestrians when exiting.

prompt.text: Morgan reaches a roundabout as a bicyclist circulates past the entry. Who yields?

answer.text: Morgan yields to the circulating bicyclist.

rationale.text: Entering traffic yields to vehicles and bicyclists already in the roundabout.

lines.text: Who has the right of way.

narration.text: This lesson covers two kinds of circular intersections: older traffic circles and modern roundabouts. The handbook describes how they differ in size and speed, which direction traffic moves in a circle, how lanes and exits work, and who has the right of way. Then it covers what to do as you approach a roundabout, enter it, travel inside it and exit. The rules for the two types are related but not identical, so watch for whether a question describes a traffic circle or a roundabout. The next lesson covers routes through roundabouts and special users such as bicyclists.

A modern roundabout is much smaller than an older traffic circle and keeps speeds low, about fifteen to twenty miles per hour, which the handbook says makes it safer. In a traffic circle, all vehicles travel counterclockwise to the right and leave by turning right. With more than one lane, get into the outside lane before your exit, and never turn right from an inside lane. So in a multi-lane traffic circle, plan your exit early by moving to the outside lane. Turning right from an inside lane would cut across the outside lane, which the handbook says never to do.

title.text: Right of way in a circle

lines.text: The whole circle is one intersection.
Circling vehicles have the right of way.
Exit right from the outside lane.

narration.text: A whole traffic circle counts as one intersection, and vehicles already in the circle have the right of way. In a traffic circle the vehicles already circulating have the right of way, and you exit only by turning right from the outside lane. So when you approach a traffic circle, traffic that is already circling goes first, and you join when there is room. Once inside, you move counterclockwise, shift to the outside lane before your exit, and leave by turning right. Questions often ask who has the right of way at the entry, and the answer is the traffic already in the circle.

lines.text: Yield to circulating vehicles and bicyclists.

narration.text: A yellow roundabout-ahead sign tells you to slow down. On entry, you yield to any vehicles or bicyclists already circulating. Vehicles inside a roundabout do not yield to those approaching. When you reach your exit, signal, and yield to pedestrians in the roundabout crosswalk. So the duties change as you move through. Approaching, you slow. Entering, you yield to circulating vehicles and bicyclists. Inside, you keep going without yielding to cars waiting to enter. Exiting, you signal and yield to pedestrians crossing at the roundabout crosswalk.

Here is the trap. Practice questions may suggest that cars inside a roundabout should stop to let waiting cars in. The handbook says the opposite. Entering roundabout traffic yields to vehicles and bicyclists already inside, while circulating traffic does not yield to approaching cars but does yield to pedestrians when exiting. So when a question asks who yields, find where each road user is. Waiting to enter means you yield. Already circulating means you continue. Exiting near a crosswalk means you yield to pedestrians. The memory line is short: entering yields, circling continues.

Here is a quick check: Morgan approaches a single-lane roundabout after passing the yellow roundabout-ahead sign. A bicyclist is already circulating and is about to pass Morgan's entry point. Who yields? Work it out before reading on. Morgan yields to the bicyclist. On entry, you yield to any vehicles or bicyclists already circulating. Once Morgan has entered, Morgan does not yield to cars waiting at the other entries, and when Morgan reaches the exit, Morgan signals and yields to any pedestrians in the roundabout crosswalk.

Let us recap. A modern roundabout is much smaller than an older traffic circle and keeps speeds around fifteen to twenty miles per hour. In a traffic circle, vehicles travel counterclockwise, the whole circle counts as one intersection, vehicles already circling have the right of way, and you exit by turning right from the outside lane, never from an inside lane. At a roundabout, slow at the yellow sign, yield on entry to vehicles and bicyclists already circulating, do not yield to approaching cars once inside, and signal and yield to pedestrians when exiting.

why_how.text: The handbook describes single-lane routes by how far around you travel, and multi-lane routes by the lane you choose before entering.
Roundabouts also have rules for emergency vehicles, bicyclists and pedestrians.

scenario.text: Taylor wants to turn left at a single-lane roundabout.

reasoning.text: In a single-lane roundabout you go three-quarters of the way around to turn left.

result.text: Taylor enters, travels three-quarters of the way around, signals and exits.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a left turn at a single-lane roundabout means cutting left across the center.

correction.text: In a single-lane roundabout three-quarters of the way around replaces a left turn, while in a multi-lane roundabout the left lane is typically used for left turns.

prompt.text: Taylor needs to turn left at a single-lane roundabout. How far around should Taylor travel?

rationale.text: In a single-lane roundabout, three-quarters of the way around replaces a left turn.

narration.text: This lesson finishes the chapter with routes through roundabouts and the rules for special road users. You will review how far around a single-lane roundabout you travel for each direction, how to choose a lane in a multi-lane roundabout, what to do when an emergency vehicle comes through, and the rules for bicyclists and pedestrians at roundabouts. The handbook describes single-lane routes as fractions of the circle and multi-lane routes by lane choice, so a question may be phrased either way. Practice translating between a destination and the route that reaches it.

lines.text: Three-quarters: left; all the way: U-turn.

narration.text: In a single-lane roundabout, you go a quarter of the way around to turn right, halfway to go straight, three-quarters of the way around to turn left, and all the way around for a U-turn. So each destination matches a fraction of the circle. When studying this rule, keep each fraction paired with its direction. Questions may name a direction and ask how far around to go, or name a fraction and ask where you will end up. Both forms test the same list from the handbook. A quarter means a right turn, and three-quarters means a left turn, as the handbook states.

lines.text: Choose from signs and markings first.
Left lane: straight, left or U-turn.

narration.text: In a multi-lane roundabout, choose your lane from signs and markings before entering. Usually the right lane is for exiting right, and the left lane is for going straight, turning left or making a U-turn. There are no lane changes inside. So in a multi-lane roundabout, the decision about where you are going happens before you enter, not after. Read the signs and pavement markings on the approach, move into the lane that serves your exit, and stay in it all the way around. The word usually matters, because posted signs and markings decide the lanes.

lines.text: Multi-lane: typically the left lane for a left.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The two kinds of roundabouts describe a left turn differently. In a single-lane roundabout three-quarters of the way around replaces a left turn, while in a multi-lane roundabout the left lane is typically used for straight, left and U-turn movements. Practice questions may offer a quarter of the way around as a left turn, which is actually the right-turn route, or suggest changing lanes inside a multi-lane roundabout, which the handbook rules out. Check which type of roundabout the question describes, then use the matching rule.

lines.text: Do not enter while an emergency vehicle passes.
Inside? Exit first, then pull over.

narration.text: Never enter a roundabout while an emergency vehicle with lights and siren is going through. If you are already inside, exit first and then pull over. Drivers should not pass a bicyclist inside a roundabout, and pedestrians should use the marked crosswalks around the outside rather than cutting through the middle. So inside a roundabout, the handbook's rules are to exit before pulling over for an emergency vehicle and to stay behind bicyclists. Pedestrians belong at the marked crosswalks around the outside of the roundabout, not crossing the center.

Here is a quick check: Taylor approaches a single-lane roundabout and wants to turn left at the intersection. After yielding to traffic already inside, Taylor enters. How far around should Taylor travel? Work it out before reading on. The answer is three-quarters of the way around. In a single-lane roundabout, a quarter of the way around is a right turn, halfway is straight, three-quarters is a left turn, and all the way around is a U-turn. Taylor travels three-quarters of the way, signals, yields to any pedestrians in the crosswalk and exits.

To finish the chapter, in a single-lane roundabout go a quarter of the way around to turn right, halfway to go straight, three-quarters to turn left and all the way around for a U-turn. In a multi-lane roundabout, choose your lane from signs and markings before entering, usually the right lane to exit right and the left lane for straight, left or U-turns, with no lane changes inside. Never enter while an emergency vehicle is going through, and if inside, exit first and then pull over. Do not pass bicyclists inside, and pedestrians use the outside crosswalks.
